si.t: WINNIPEG HOUSE PURCHASE — FINANCIAL MODEL TEMPLATE
A blank, reusable model for deciding how much house to buy in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and how to finance it.
All Manitoba and federal rules are built in and sourced. No personal data of any kind is included.
1. Go to the 'Assumptions' tab. Fill in every BLUE cell. YELLOW-filled cells are the ones that move the answer most.
2. Everything else recalculates automatically. Do not overwrite black cells.
3. Read the tabs in this order: Affordability -> Scenarios -> Closing Costs -> Rent vs Buy -> Down Payment -> RRSP-HBP.
BLUE text = an input. You type here.
YELLOW fill = key lever. Changing it moves the answer a lot.
BLACK text = calculated. Do not overwrite.
GREEN text = pulled from another tab.
Assumptions Every input in one place. Start here.
Reference Data Manitoba and federal rules, rates and market data, with sources. Update quarterly.
Affordability What a lender would approve (stress-tested GDS/TDS) vs what you can comfortably carry.
Scenarios 5% / 10% / 20% / 25% down compared side by side at your target price.
Closing Costs Cash required on closing day beyond the down payment.

THE EXAMPLE HOUSEHOLD ALREADY IN THE FILE
The model ships pre-filled so you can see it working. Overwrite column B on the Assumptions tab with your own
numbers; column C keeps the example beside it for reference. The sample household is:
Two applicants earning $75,000 and $45,000 — $120,000 gross combined
$50,000 saved: $16,000 FHSA, $18,000 TFSA, $8,000 RRSP, $6,000 non-registered, $2,000 cash
A $550/month car loan, no other debt
Targeting a $350,000 home with 10% down over 30 years, first-time buyers
Currently paying $1,500/month rent, saving $1,200/month, planning to stay 10 years
- TDS binds, not GDS. The car loan — not housing cost — is what limits this household's approval.
- At 10% down, CMHC insurance costs them roughly $10,400, added to the mortgage and carried for 30 years.
- Cash to close is about $48,500 against $50,000 saved. Almost nothing left over. This is the single most
common miss: budgeting the down payment and forgetting that closing costs are separate and due the same day.
- A lender would approve far more than they can comfortably carry. Both numbers sit side by side on purpose.
THE TWO THINGS MOST BUYERS GET WRONG
1. They anchor on what the lender approves instead of what they can comfortably carry. The gap is usually large.
The Affordability tab shows both numbers side by side on purpose.
2. They compare rent vs buy over too short a horizon. Transaction costs are fixed, so the break-even is typically
5-7 years. The Rent vs Buy tab solves for the break-even rather than assuming one.
Rates, prices and tax brackets change. Every figure on the Reference Data tab is dated and sourced -
re-check them before relying on this model. This is a planning tool, not financial, tax or legal advice.

RENT vs BUY — terminal wealth comparison, with optional factors you can switch on and off
OPTIONAL FACTORS — set 1 to include, 0 to exclude
If owning costs more per month than renting, the renter banks the difference and invests it. If renting costs more, the buyer does. Switching this OFF assumes the difference is simply spent.
OFF sets appreciation to 0% and tests whether buying stands up in a flat market on its own merits.
The buyer sinks this into the house. The renter invests it. This is the fair starting point for both.
Includes the full mortgage payment — principal as well as interest. That is real cash leaving the account each month.
Positive = owning costs more, so the RENTER has this much spare to invest. Negative = the BUYER does.
Difference invested at your expected return. Contributions credited at year end (slightly conservative).
Only fills if renting is the more expensive option.
Home equity, net of selling cost
TERMINAL WEALTH — what each path is actually worth
Home equity plus anything the buyer was able to invest.
The up-front capital compounded, plus the invested monthly difference.
HOW THE TWO SWITCHES CHANGE THE ANSWER
SWITCH 1 — investing the monthly difference. This is the factor most rent-vs-buy calculators quietly omit,
and it usually matters more than appreciation. If owning costs $1,100/month more than renting, a disciplined
renter investing that gap accumulates a large portfolio. Leaving it OFF assumes the renter simply spends the
difference — which is what most people actually do, but it is an assumption about behaviour, not arithmetic.
Turn it ON for the honest financial comparison. Turn it OFF to model a renter who does not invest.
SWITCH 2 — appreciation. With it ON you are forecasting the housing market, which nobody does reliably.
Turn it OFF to see whether buying stands up on shelter costs and forced savings alone. If buying only wins
with appreciation switched on, you are betting on price growth rather than buying a place to live.
WHAT THE MODEL DOES NOT CAPTURE — and these favour BUYING:
- In Canada, gains on a principal residence are 100% TAX-FREE. Investment gains are not. If the investment
return above is a pre-tax figure, the comparison is unfairly tilted toward renting. Use an after-tax number.
- Forced savings. A mortgage payment is compulsory; investing the difference is optional and most people
do not sustain it for 10 years. The model assumes perfect discipline from the renter.
- Security of tenure, freedom to renovate, and no landlord risk. Real, but not financial.
- A mortgage is leveraged. You control the whole asset having put down a fraction of its value.
WHAT IT DOES NOT CAPTURE THAT FAVOURS RENTING:
- Liquidity and mobility. Selling costs roughly 5% and takes months.
- Concentration risk. A house is one undiversified asset in one city.
- Special assessments, major repairs, and the risk that maintenance exceeds the 1%/yr reserve.
This assumes one rate for the whole amortization. In reality you renew every 3-5 years at the rate available then.
RENEWAL RISK is the largest unmodelled risk in any Canadian mortgage. Re-run with the rate set to 6% and 7%.
If a 7% renewal breaks your budget, buy less house.
DOWN PAYMENT — where the money comes from, and what it costs to get it
FUNDING WATERFALL — draw in this order

No tax, no opportunity cost beyond the interest forgone.

LAST RESORT — triggers capital gains tax. Sell losing positions first to harvest offsetting losses.
Only the GAIN is taxed, at a 50% inclusion rate — not the whole proceeds.
Sell losing positions first: realized losses offset realized gains. Watch the 30-day superficial loss rule.

Money needed within 2 years does not belong in equities. Move it to a HISA or a GIC ladder.

RRSP → HOME BUYERS' PLAN — the contribute, deduct, withdraw strategy
1. Contribute cash you ALREADY HOLD (from a TFSA or non-registered account) into an RRSP, up to your unused room.
2. Claim the deduction. The refund equals your contribution x your marginal tax rate.
3. WAIT AT LEAST 90 DAYS. Funds withdrawn sooner are NOT HBP-eligible and become fully taxable income.
4. Withdraw up to the HBP limit per person — completely tax-free.
5. Use it as your down payment. Repay 1/15th per year, starting the 2nd year after withdrawal.
Net effect: the same money still becomes your down payment, and you keep the tax refund for having routed it
through the RRSP. The cost is a 15-year obligation to repay the money into your own retirement account.
This only helps if you have unused RRSP room AND cash sitting outside registered accounts. Check both.
From your CRA Notice of Assessment or My Account. Unused room carries forward indefinitely.

- THE 90-DAY RULE IS ABSOLUTE. Contribute at least 90 days before you need the funds. Plan backwards from closing.
- Lenders separately require ~90 days of account history proving down payment funds are yours. The two rules stack.
- Verify your real RRSP room on your Notice of Assessment. Do not guess.
- Contribute in your HIGHEST-income year — the deduction is worth exactly your marginal rate.
- If one applicant earns much more, a SPOUSAL RRSP may capture the higher deduction on both halves.
Spousal HBP withdrawals are permitted, but confirm the attribution treatment with an accountant first.
- You must be a first-time buyer, and must buy or build by 1 October of the year AFTER the withdrawal.
- DO NOT do this at the expense of the FHSA. The FHSA is deductible going in AND tax-free coming out,
with no repayment obligation at all. It strictly dominates the RRSP for a first home.
PRIORITY ORDER: 1) Max the FHSA -> 2) RRSP via HBP -> 3) TFSA -> 4) non-registered.
